formationLabel: Lithuanian Catholic society linked to a church project by 1911 · first completed church reported in 1916 · institution closed, exact canonical formation and terminal mechanics unresolved
currentUse: The Diocese of Syracuse lists St. Joseph in Binghamton as closed and directs its sacramental records to the Church of the Holy Trinity. Secondary histories report a final Mass in 2003 and sale of the 1 Judson Avenue church in 2008. Later public records place Grace Tabernacle and then a New York State residential program at 1 Judson Avenue, but the reviewed evidence does not prove how much of the 1949-1950 church fabric survives or its current interior condition.
summary: St. Joseph was Binghamton's Lithuanian Roman Catholic parish. A Lithuanian society bought 315 Clinton Street for a church project in 1911, but that project was abandoned and the property became a separate association hall rather than the parish church. A first completed church is reported in 1916, followed by a new church at 1 Judson Avenue in 1949-1950. The parish is officially closed and its records are held by Holy Trinity; sources distinguish a 2003 final Mass from the 2008 sale of the Judson property. The former church site's present physical condition remains unresolved.

historicalNarrative.text: Binghamton's Lithuanian Catholics organized through the St. Joseph Lithuanian Society before the parish had a completed church. A National Register nomination identifies the society as a parent organization of St. Joseph Lithuanian Church and says it bought 315 Clinton Street in 1911 to construct a church. This establishes a parish-linked project, not a completed worship site or a canonical erection date.

The Clinton Street church project was abandoned in 1917 and the unfinished property was sold. The Lithuanian National Association then completed its own hall at 315 Clinton Street, a separate civic and cultural building that served Lithuanian organizations until its 1964 sale to Tri-Cities Opera. The hall's relationship to the society does not make it a St. Joseph worship site.

historicalNarrative.text: Secondary field documentation reports that a completed first St. Joseph church was built in 1916 on the opposite side of the later Judson Avenue site. A separate site history says this older church became the parish hall in 1952. Because the accepted public sources do not give a precise street number or deed, the first church remains a distinct but incompletely located site.

historicalNarrative.text: The later church at 1 Judson Avenue was built in 1949-1950. Field documentation records Lithuanian inscriptions and religious art on the modern facade, while the secondary site history dates the dedication to February 5, 1950. These are building milestones, not evidence that the parish itself began in 1950.

historicalNarrative.text: The end of separate parish worship and the disposition of the building are different events. A secondary site history reports a final Mass on November 16, 2003; field documentation says the church was closed and sold to Grace Tabernacle in 2008. The Diocese of Syracuse now lists St. Joseph as closed and directs its sacramental records to Holy Trinity, but it does not publish an effective closure date or merger instrument.

historicalNarrative.text: The 1 Judson Avenue property continued through later uses. A 2009 obituary placed a memorial service at Grace Tabernacle there, and a current New York State procurement page lists the address as a Broome DDSOO residential-program site. These address-level records show post-parish occupancy but do not establish the present condition of the 1949-1950 church fabric or its interior.

conflictsWithArchiveRecord: The inherited 1916 formation value is supportable only as the reported first completed church, not yet as a canonical parish-erection date. The 2003 final Mass and 2008 sale describe different events. The official diocesan directory confirms closure but does not resolve the exact terminal date or mechanism. The Lithuanian National Association Hall at 315 Clinton Street is a separate civic property, not the completed St. Joseph parish church.
gaps: The exact parish erection instrument and date; the exact address and fate of the 1916 church; whether any portion of the abandoned 315 Clinton Street church project was used for worship; the closure or consolidation decree; the interval between the 2003 final Mass and 2008 sale; the canonical status of Holy Trinity continuity beyond records custody and secondary descriptions; the current physical and interior condition of the 1 Judson church fabric; and any parish cemetery remain unresolved.
